subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPRESSION OF VIEW ON APARTHEID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in asking the
Prime Minister whether he can report to the house on the steps that have been taken to protect the interests of a Canadian citizen, Mr. Norman Phillips, arrested in South Africa for carrying out his duties as newspaper reporter, may I also ask him a related question supplementing those I previously asked on March 25 and 31, namely whether he would make provision, as was done last Friday in the parliament at Westminster, so the views of this parliament can be expressed, through a resolution, on the policy of apartheid.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPRESSION OF VIEW ON APARTHEID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the first question is concerned, when information was received by the government to the effect that a Canadian newspaperman, Mr. Norman Phillips, was being detained, the matter was taken up with me, acting in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and as a result the Canadian High Commissioner was instructed to inform the South African government that the arrest and detention of Mr. Phillips could not but add to the widespread public indignation already felt in Canada at the measures which had given rise to recent violence and loss of life in South Africa.
The high commissioner was instructed to make strong representation to the South African government with a view to securing the release of Mr. Phillips. Those representations were made. While I am not in a position at the moment to report finally as to what the result may be, I have reason to hope that Mr. Phillips will be released from detention.

Inquiries of the Ministry There is however, a suggestion that to that release may be added an indication on the part of the South Africa government that Mr. Phillips' presence in that country would no longer be considered desirable by the government of South Africa.
In so far as the second question is concerned, the Leader of the Opposition has referred to a resolution which came before the House of Commons of Great Britain on Friday last. If the house would allow me I might refer to the pertinent portions of that resolution:
That this house, deploring the present racialist policies now being pursued by South African government, under which non-Europeans are consistently denied normal human and political rights, including the right of campaigning for a peaceful change in the laws under which they live, and the recent declaration of a state of emergency and the many arbitrary arrests, fearing that a continuation of this repression is threatening the security and welfare of all races living in Union of South Africa and good relation between members of the commonwealth, urges Her Majesty's government to take the opportunity at the forthcoming commonwealth prime ministers' conference to bring home to South African government the strong feelings of British people; and restates its firm belief that peace and tranquility in South Africa can only be secured in the long run on the basis of freedom and equality and a full respect for the inherent dignity and humanity of all men.
Now, sir, speaking on behalf of the government and people of Canada, I have stated that we deplore the situation which brought about the bloodshed in South Africa. I have stated that whatever one's personal feelings may be-and I do not have to state what mine are in this regard, for they have been stated and restated in the past-respect must be had for the situation which might arise in a commonwealth prime ministers' conference if in advance there was an indication that this matter would be included in the discussions. There is no official agenda for the prime ministers' conferences, but I am sure hon. members will realize that in the informality that prevails at those conferences, and with the prime ministers of India, Pakistan, Ceylon, Ghana, Malaya, and other countries of the commonwealth present, it may certainly be expected that the views of the various commonwealth governments will be made most clearly evident.
The Leader of the Opposition asked whether an opportunity might be given for the introduction and discussion of such a resolution as was brought before the United Kingdom House of Commons three days ago. While there is no opportunity now, having regard to the order paper, the fact that we are discussing the budget and also the fact that we have fully before us the very tragic happening of last Saturday, I can say that immediately after recess, when
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

the condition of affairs in South Africa will at least not be as turbulent, we hope, as it is at the moment, we might then give consideration to doing that which the hon. member has suggested so that the views of Canada's House of Commons, with respect to which there is no difference from the point of view of party affiliation or position in the house, might be expressed.
I would also point out that if I were not sitting where I am, with the responsibilities that are mine, I would express myself somewhat differently from the way I am at the moment. But looking ahead to the prime ministers' conference, while there must be the clearest consideration and the frankest discussion of those things that affect all parts of the commonwealth, and though bound together by no pact or treaty we are free to discuss as we will, I fear for the future of the commonwealth if, while never failing to make clear the viewpoint of each of us, the prime ministers' conference should become the judge and jury of the conduct of member nations.
In saying that I also express the hope- my predecessors Mr. King and Mr. St. Laurent have also spoken strongly of this matter-that while there should be nothing done among the member nations to cause division and dissension, some day the members of this great group of nations will be able to bring about a declaration of basic, accepted principles with regard to human dignity so that together all the nations of the commonwealth, having a similar heritage, may hold, in so far as these basic, fundamental things that touch sacredness of the human person are concerned, a common basis for agreement.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPRESSION OF VIEW ON APARTHEID
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I will not be out of order, or if I am you will excuse me, if I express the appreciation of our party on the Prime Minister's statement that an opportunity will be found at the earliest convenient date to express the views of this parliament on apartheid through a resolution. May I also express the view that this resolution should include an expression of the hope of this parliament that, before it is too late, some way out of the distressing situation in South Africa may be found, before further violence makes any peaceful solution, founded on right and justice, impossible.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPRESSION OF VIEW ON APARTHEID
speechtext: Speaking on behalf of a party that abhors violence in all its forms, 1 want to say we support the proposal made by the leader of the official opposition that this house be given an opportunity to discuss the South African

situation, such as was provided to members of the House of Commons at Westminster. We have evidence once again, Mr. Speaker, of the fact that Britain leads the world in speaking with a united voice against tyranny.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that while we are glad to hear the Prime Minister's statement that at a later date we will have an opportunity of taking a course of action similar to that taken in Great Britain, we would prefer him to take that action now so we can support Great Britain's united stand in opposition to typranny in South Africa.
Before I sit down I should like also to say that the attempted assassination of the South African prime minister was a most unfortunate event. This attempt on his life is evidence of a grave social conflict arising from the practice of tyranny in South Africa. So long as this tyranny remains there can be no peace in the hearts of freedom loving people of the commonwealth or elsewhere in the world. We suggest, Mr. Speaker, that now is the time for the Prime Minister of Canada to speak up for Canada.

May I ask
a supplementary question. Can the Prime Minister say whether Canada has been approached by any country or any group of countries with regard to the suggestion that a special assembly of the United Nations be held regarding this matter?

I cannot say definitely, although the information I have would not bear out this suggestion on the part of the hon. gentleman. I would ask to be allowed also to say to the hon. member for Kootenay West that the Prime Minister's views have always been made known with regard to these matters that are concerned with discrimination, and those views have never been muted. However, at a time like this outspoken criticisms may have the effect of making the situation more serious, deplorable as it already is. It is for this reason that there has been, on the part of this government, a sense of restrained responsibility, without failing to recognize the needs of the moment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister a supplementary question. maintopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is not the situation Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is confused. He is referring perhaps to a news dispatch which I saw, I think, in a newspaper on Friday last-

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Saturday's Winnipeg Free Press.

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
This news dispatch evidently made no distinction between the canned pork we are holding and fresh pork. I should like to remind the hon. member and the house that on March 8, as reported at page 1836 of Hansard, I announced that starting April
Inquiries of the Ministry 18 the stabilization board would offer stocks of canned pork-may I emphasize "canned pork"-for sale in the domestic market.
At that time I also stated that it was not expected that the sale of canned pork into the domestic market would have any significant influence on the hog market, the reason being that canned pork is a specialty product representing only a very small portion of the total pork sales, and does not compete directly with the normal sale of fresh and cured pork products.
Further, now that pork products may move freely between Canada and the United States, the most important influence in determining hog prices in Canada is the price level in the United States and, regardless of the volume of offerings of Canadian product, hog prices will not drop below the general level of the United States market.
Actually this is a straight matter of putting back into the market products which we purchased when we were under the old form of price support. As I am sure hon. members realize, it would be completely uneconomic for the government to hold millions of pounds of canned pork and for packers to can more when they are able to sell in the market all the fresh pork they are now securing from current hog deliveries.

speechtext: This is the consequence of the government's repudiation of policy.

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT

I refer to canned pork, of course.
The amount of canned pork we now hold will be released into the market in keeping with the demand for it. The canned pork we have left will not be thrown on the market in one fell swoop, but will be fed into the market gradually as and when the market is able to absorb it without having any effect on current hog prices.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, debate on the budget fortunately allows one to comment not only on what the budget contains but on what it does not contain. The budget seems to lean toward the latter to such a degree that it could in fact be called the vacuum budget.

The Budget-Mr. Granger
However, there was a nostalgic reminder of the past in the budget speech. Certainly when the Minister of Finance praised the qualities of thrift it was like a voice from the past. "Thrift" is a word we do not hear much nowadays, and I thought it might have been dropped from the English language. During the golden age of Liberalism it was not needed much, but like other words which have fallen into disuse-"unemployment", for instance-it has been been brought back into current usage by the Conservatives. Doubtless the language is the richer for it, even if the people are the poorer.
Thrift is doubtless a good thing. There is no doubt but that many of us would be better off-if we practised it, or if we made it a motto to make things do and to wear them out, but what would happen to an economy based on spending I would hesitate to say. Certainly there are many people in Canada today who have to practise thrift whether they like to or not.
The rosy description of our soundly based economy was heartening, and no doubt it must be comforting to the multitude of unemployed to know they are living in the midst of such prosperity. However, it is not considered good form to mention unemployment. In fact, to do so is to court the charge of being a Jeremiah. Unemployment must be ignored. Officially it does not exist.
I noted with interest what the hon. member for St. John's East said regarding the position of Canadian citizens working on United States bases. I am pleased, as he is, to hear that their status in respect to pension rights has been recognized. I trust that this includes those working on the Goose Bay air base in Labrador. I feel I should point out that the base in Labrador was not included in the original bases deal, and part of the air base at Labrador has been leased by the Canadian government to the United States under different circumstances.
I also noted with interest the hon. gentleman's comments on vocational training. I would ask him to use his influence with the Minister of Labour to adopt the proposals of the Liberal party as put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, namely that the federal government should itself bear the full cost of vocational training for the unemployed instead of trying to push half of it on the provinces which already provide the vocational training schools.
So much has been said over the years about the fisheries, and particularly the salt codfish section of the industry, that I rather hesitate to discuss it further. But I believe so strongly in the importance to Canada of the fishing industry that I ask the patience


of the house while I refer again to Canada's oldest industry, which is still very valuable and which can be much more valuable in the future, both to Canada as a whole and to the individual fishermen.
From time immemorial fishing, like farming, has been one of the basic industries of mankind. The fisheries were very important to the countries of Europe away back in 1497, when John Cabot sighted Bonavista and in reality discovered Canada. When he returned to England he reported that the waters of the new found land were full of fish, and the very next year English merchants were outfitting ships to voyage across the Atlantic to the new fishing grounds. Soon the French, the Portuguese, the Basques and the Spanish were fishing in the waters of the new world. From that day to this the waters of Canada's east coast have been fished by many nations. Today, as in the closing days of the fifteenth century, the flags of many nations dot the seas off the coasts of Newfoundland and Labrador, and over the years the fishing industry has been a very important factor in the economy of eastern Canada.
However, less attention is paid to the fisheries today than in the past. There is reason for this. The industrialization of central Canada, the wealth which industry has brought, and the huge agricultural industry of the west have drawn public interest away from the old maritime pursuits, the fisheries of the Atlantic provinces. This is understandable, but it could be fatal to a large segment of our population. I do not dispute for a moment the right of the more prosperous and populous parts of Canada to press their problems and to advertise their progress. Rather, I applaud them for it. As Canadians we are all proud of the might of industrial Canada and of the glorious productivity of our land. What I do regret is the lack of public support for an industry which is vital to the survival of the Atlantic provinces.
It has been said in criticism that if the fishing industry cannot support itself it had better disappear; that if fishermen cannot make a living catching fish they should get better jobs elsewhere. On the face of it such criticism appears to be just. In any case, that is what is happening; and if the trend continues-and the downward trend is confined not only to the fisheries-the end will be the depression and depopulation of the Atlantic provinces. But in a nation growing at the rate Canada is growing we cannot afford to let any industry disappear. Every part of our national wealth must be exploited, and the waters off the northeastern coast of Canada are wealthy with food. There is no need for

the Atlantic provinces to be a depressed area; there is no need for the fishing industry to disappear.
It is granted that the industry is an old one, but age in itself is no yardstick of vitality. For instance, the wine industry is one of the oldest in the world, but today it is not considered to be a bad investment. The fishing industry has had its ups and downs, but so has every other industry. The real trouble, sir, is first, that the fishing industry has changed too litte over the years; it has failed to embrace modern methods quickly enough; second, it is facing heavily subsidized competition. Canadian fishermen must compete with the Portuguese, the French, the Icelanders, the Russians and many others, all of whom have the benefits of substantial government subsidies. Somehow we must effectively solve these two problems.
With respect to the former, the need for modernization of the fisheries, much has been done in recent years. We can take some satisfaction from the vast changes which have taken place. True, they came late but much progress has been made in the industrialization of the fisheries in recent years. Prior to the last decade or two there had been very little change in the way of catching fish. Looking through an old history of Newfoundland some years ago I saw some old drawings of fishermen of the sixteenth century, showing gear, stages, dress, and so on, and I was shocked to note that little change had taken place. To try to operate a fishing industry today, using ancient methods, is like trying to run a modern farm with hand implements, like attempting to meet the world need for grain with hoes and the single furrow plow.
It is no wonder that fishermen found it difficult to make ends meet and often quit the sea to get jobs ashore. But in recent years, and almost too late, the cod fishery has been partially industrialized. With provincial and federal aid modern plants have been built, handling both fresh and salt fish, and where these plants are operating the way of life has changed. While the industrialization of the fisheries was getting under way many fishermen quit the fisheries. Young men are not making fishing their profession because of the bad economic history of the industry. I am convinced that a danger point is being reached. Industrialization has come too late to save the industry without additional steps being taken to complete its rehabilitation. While a commercial revolution has been taking place, the fishermen have been disappearing. I would impress this upon hon. members. You can make a farmer into a miner, you can make a labourer into a mechanic, but a deep sea fisherman has to be bred to the job.
79951-0-196J
The Budget-Mr. Granger
Now, mark you, most fishermen and sons of fishermen would prefer to follow the sea, with its freedom and rich experience. This is not just a pretty story but is in fact the truth. I have met many fishermen and sailors who want to continue to follow the sea, but who quit it because they could not make a living at it. While the good effects of the industrialization of the fisheries are spreading out to the remote areas, something must be done to encourage fishermen to continue fishing, to make it possible for them to continue fishing, or one of these days we will find ourselves with modern plants and no fish for them. If we lose a generation of fishermen we will lose a great industry in Canada.
But this need not be so. Action can be taken to save the industry, speed up the industrialization and make a profit for Canada. The good work being done by the federal Department of Fisheries and the provincial department of fisheries in research, active aid, and so forth must of course be continued. But of immediate concern is making money available to fishermen so they can continue to fish.
Let me illustrate. On the Labrador coast today-and the waters of Labrador are one of the great sources of supply; I will come back to this later-there are many fishermen who have lost stages and fishing property through storms. Their boats and gear are worn out. Salmon nets are ragged; cod traps are full of holes. It is beyond the ability of the fishermen to get the necessary materials to repair their nets and traps, to build new boats, to buy engines and equip themselves to be able to prosecute the fisheries efficiently. It is impossible for them to do this without help. There is need, and need now, for active federal assistance to fishermen to replace worn-out gear.
Money must be made available by loan or grant to see them through this difficult period. Present loan schemes are neither ample nor workable. Capital must be made available. It must be made easier for fishermen to get up to date equipment. Believe me, it will pay the nation to do this. The community stage program must be continued and extended. It must include Labrador, because the fishing plants of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland have to look more and more to Labrador for their supply. Within a few years I predict that Labrador will be more important than ever to the fishing industry. If we do not recognize what the Russians and others are even now capitalizing on we will regret it forever. At all costs there must be more attention paid to the Labrador fisheries. The replacement of property is of tremendous

The Budget-Mr. Granger importance. Several of these community stages must be built in Labrador this year.
The bait service, considerably improved, must be extended rapidly. A perennial shortage of bait has cost this country untold millions over the years. Research into artificial bait should be stepped up. The building of more fish plants must be encouraged. There must be more fish plants, with more fishermen fishing more efficiently and making more money per man. These things can be done at comparatively little cost. Let me repeat that the two great enemies of our oldest industry are tardiness in accepting change and the heavy government subsidies paid to our competitors. Certainly we can beat them both.
However, the fate of the industry rests right here. Only if the representatives of all of Canada make the fishermen's business their business and the Atlantic provinces' business their business can we hope to save a vital industry and a noble region of Canada. If for no other reason, national pride should make us want to do something about looking after our own interests.
Last fall while I was in northern Newfoundland there was a large ship and a flotilla of smaller ships inside the Grey islands. They proved to be a Russian supply ship and a fleet of Russian trawlers. It is known that Russian ships were still fishing in Labrador waters in February of last year. French and Portuguese trawlers come into St. Anthony for supplies. And I could go on. The ships of many nations are fishing Newfoundland and Labrador waters. In summer in my home town of Catalina on the northeast coast, sometimes the bay outside the harbour looks like a city as the lighted ships of a foreign fleet fish at night inside the three mile limit. Canadian waters are a happy hunting ground for the nations which know the value of the wealth in our waters. This is something that most Canadians apparently do not know and, what is worse, do not seem to care about. I think the proposed 10-year delay in protecting fishing rights in our coastal waters is regrettable and dangerous.
We stand to lose our fishing industry on the northeast coast of Canada. We stand to let the Labrador waters be lost to Canada in every practical sense. I say we cannot afford it. No matter how wealthy Canada is, she cannot afford it. The cost of rebuilding and making the Labrador fishery profitable is trifling compared with the reward. I say we cannot afford not to do this; and yet the Labrador coast is neglected. Despite the trifling cost of inexpensive radiotelephone sets, the fisher folk have little or no means of


communication. They try to survive under primitive conditions, without aid or interest, while the efficient ships of Russia reap the wealth of their waters.
However, while the coasts of Labrador await the attention necessary to development, the interior of Labrador, practically unknown and unexplored since creation, is now beginning to yield up its secrets and its wealth. The developments now in process in this unknown territory promise to make it one of the most important and wealthiest parts of Canada and, indeed, of the world.
A great change has taken place in the public attitude toward this unknown land in recent years, though I do not believe the scope of exploration and development is yet fully appreciated. Early explorers were astonished by the forbidding, fortress-like coasts of Labrador, the vastness of the Labrador wilderness and the barrenness of its northern mountains. It was early dubbed "the land which God gave to Cain". In 1770 Captain George Cartwright, who voyaged to Labrador, wrote:
One is insensibly drawn to the conclusion that this country was the last which God made, and that He had no other view than to throw together there the refuse of His materials as of no use to mankind.
However, despite that bitter observation Cartwright continued to voyage to Labrador for 16 years, and it is interesting to note in his journal that he thought he had detected the presence of iron ore. There were valuable materials in what Cartwright called the refuse of creation, for today the iron ore deposits of Labrador are of unimaginable importance to the economy of North America. In my opinion Cartwright did not do justice to this vast and impressive land, for no one can visit Labrador without being impressed by its grandeur, its iron-ribbed strength and its brooding immensity. In Hamilton inlet, where the great fortress of Goose Bay is located, even the weather is extremely good.
In recent years a modern saga of exploration has taken place in the Labrador. The bush plane on floats or skis, the men with sleeping bags and parkas, are the modern pioneers of a new front for civilization. There was little in the way of recorded data to go on, but huge deposits of iron ore and great potentials of water power were thoroughly investigated.
The water power of Hamilton falls is stupendous. The capacity is estimated to be about four million horsepower or more, with a possibility of another two million horsepower being available after the upper water power has been developed. That is a potential of six million horsepower, and the lower tributaries may well add another five million

horsepower. The British Newfoundland Corporation has spent several million in exploratory work, and in 1956 an access road was built from the Quebec, South Shore and Labrador Railway to the Hamilton river, a distance of 104 miles. I might add that 56 miles of this road were graded to a standard adequate to handle wheeled traffic.
This year the company will build a 120,000 horsepower hydro plant near Hamilton falls. The surveys have been completed and the preliminary work started. The project, including transmission lines, is scheduled to be finished in 1962. The power generated by this plant will be used at the new iron mines which are opening up in the Wabush lake area of Labrador, 110 miles away. Thus two of the great natural resources of Labrador have been linked together. The Iron Ore Company of Canada and Wabush Iron Company Limited will be the customers.
The great iron ore deposits of Labrador are being developed. A railway is being built there. A pilot plant is in operation. A town is springing up, and soon in what was once wilderness a modern town of several thousand people, with modern schools, hospitals and all the appurtenances of civilization, will live, move and have its being in what was once a remote and unknown land. It may be that God did not give this land to Cain after all; he gave it to Canada.
Here are northern development and the northern vision being fulfilled. We have heard much about visions and northern development during the past two years, but while the great northern vision of the administration seems to be fading like a disturbing mirage, in Labrador there is vision and fulfilment. I am not one to scoff at vision. I deplore the lack of it. The proof of what vision and patience can do exists today in Labrador. It is a great vindication of the vision of the premier of Newfoundland and others who believed in the practicability of northern development.
I would hate to see the northern vision, of which we heard so much during the prophetic winter days of 1958, die until the need for prophecy arises again. I believe the northern vision must go to meet the northern lights in Labrador. Here is a great new country of proven wealth. Here are known resources to be developed. Here is a region so large that a great agency like the federal government is needed to bring it the necessary public services. Here is a need for roads to known resources. Here is a place for federal enterprise in opening up a great new and wealthy land. Federal roads to resources, such as a road from Seven Islands on
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy the St. Lawrence to Goose Bay, Labrador- these are the things to inspire and challenge the vision of a great new northern development even now coming lustily alive.
I have talked much of Labrador, Mr. Speaker, and of the old industry declining on its coast as well as the new industry beginning to flourish in its interior. Both have a great potential for our nation, and I am sure all Canadians, as they get to know this new land of Labrador, will be proud to count it as part of their country, even as I am proud to be its representative in parliament.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first to congratulate the Minister of Finance and this government upon the budget. Being one who is proud of at least some of the thinking of my Scottish ancestors, it gives me very great satisfaction to see that the forecast is that we will come out on the right side of the ledger. Those in responsibility on this side of the house have every right to be proud of the fact that they have directed the public affairs of this nation and given the leadership necessary to bring us through a period of difficulty. Now we are in a position to indicate to the people of this country that they can look forward to prosperity and development on a pay as you go basis.
The position we have now reached as a nation has not come about by mere chance but is the fruit of careful planning and prudence, coupled with the unselfish application of the resources of our people in every walk of life. It is gratifying also to observe, especially during the last few years, not only the growth and progress economically but also the trend toward moulding a more united nation, made up of so many ethnic groups and based upon our British and French heritage. Let those who have assumed responsibility, and indeed this should include every citizen of this country, not accept all these blessings lightly and become complacent. There are many influences around us which, if we are not on our guard, will seek to destroy the high standards and principles which have become ours, not only through our own efforts but as a result of the sacrifices of those who pioneered in this great country.
In the last few years there has been a tendency for more and more people to call upon the government to enter more and more into business and private lives. I hasten to point out that it is generally recognized that the more we demand from government, the more of our individual freedom we sacrifice. The strength of a nation, I submit, lies not

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy in regimentation and control but in the initiative and industrious capabilities of the individual, working in an atmosphere of free enterprise.
The geographical location and nature of this country while having many advantages, also has some disadvantages. First, Canada stretching across the northerly part of North America is subject to extremes in seasonal climatic conditions, and this tends to raise many difficulties in the competitive production of many of the goods required on world markets. Because of this fact we have always been faced with a problem in providing year-round production in many things and this results, of course, in the problem of maintaining steady and full employment for all classes of workmen. Our climatic factor also concedes advantages in the seasonal production of various items to our great neighbour to the south and, in this regard, contributes in no small way to the present trade deficit with our neighbour. If we are to continue to enjoy the luxury of many consumer goods which because of climatic conditions can be produced earlier or only in the south, we must contiually open up new developments here and streamline production in such a manner that we can sell more to bring our trade ledger more into balance.
Second, this country stretching from sea to sea for a distance of nearly 4,000 miles has many transportation problems. The bulk of our population and manufacturing industries have been concentrated in the mid-eastern section. This, of course, has created many difficulties, both in distribution and marketing, for the lesser populated areas which lie in 'the western and Atlantic areas. If, for example, we who live in the Atlantic provinces are to develop our economy and enjoy the full resources of the country, it is necessary that steps are taken to realistically equalize this cost of distribution so it will be shared by all Canadians. When this great country was brought together in confederation it was intended that all citizens should share equal rights and privileges. Since that time we have shouldered the burden imposed by protective tariffs, and we in the Atlantic provinces have not been afforded equal treatment in that we have been, and still are, bearing additional burdens brought about by continued costs in transportation.
Before confederation, because of access to the water trade routes of the world, transportation was not a problem. However, after confederation tariffs robbed us of access to this trade in order to protect manufacturing which was mostly located in central Canada. Import tariffs, the benefits of which accrue to the national treasury, are nothing more

than a form of subsidization, because the one who buys the product thus assessed pays the shot. Why then, I might ask, are we who live in the extremities of the country not entitled to subsidization which would make us equal in the other respects?
For example, let us look at the distribution of products which are manufactured locally but sold on a national scale. It is my considered opinion that if it is not reasonably possible or practical economically to diversify some of these factors, then the products produced in this manner should bear the same price tags at distribution points all across the country. For example, let us consider the standard automobile. The standard automobile costs over $100 more in Windsor, Nova Scotia than it does in Windsor, Ontario. If these prices were equalized it would only mean a slight increase to the many buyers in Ontario, but would mean a major reduction in price to the buyers in the extreme areas.

A good deal has been said during this debate with regard to the government's attitude toward the civil service. Some of those affected in my constituency express pleasure in that, since this government has taken office, they have already received two substantial pay increases and a good medical plan for which the government pays half the cost. The empty arguments of some hon. members opposite only show that they still have not learned that grass is better fodder than brass.
Hon. members opposite have had a good deal to say with regard to Canada's participation in continental defence. Surely they must realize that we are receiving a great degree of protection in view of our modest contribution. It is unthinkable that the people of this country could bear the burden of a go it alone plan. If they examine the present arrangement carefully they will find that under the policy of this government we are not only receiving reasonable defence but are also sharing in the production program to a extent which means a great deal to the economy of our country. In this age of missiles and electronics, techniques and defensive designs are changing so rapidly that the implements under development are liable to be obsolete before they reach the practical stage. It is therefore necessary to gamble to a certain extent beyond the foreseeable future.
Some hon. members opposite, in being critical of our program, seem to forget the colossal blunders made by the former government when they sat with it on this side of the house. I wish to remind them of one which hits close to home. For instance, the establishment of Camp Gagetown in New Brunswick, at a terrific cost to the public, certainly could not be justified, and so far as I am concerned involved the spending of huge sums of taxpayers' money and resulted in the ruination of the economy of such communities as Debert and Aldershot in Nova Scotia where facilities to meet the required military need already existed to a large extent.
Earlier I referred to our trade deficit with other countries. It is to be noted that we also have a considerable deficit in our tourist spending. It would be a terrific boost to our economy if we could encourage our own people to spend their vacation dollars within the boundaries of this country and, as a matter of fact, it should be possible to attract more tourists from other countries. I wonder whether we in the Atlantic provinces have explored all the possibilities. I am thinking at the moment particularly of the hundreds of miles of ideal bathing beaches along our shore lines, which I daresay are practically
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy unknown to the people a few miles inland. If hon. members of this house and their families have an opportunity to spend a week or two in partaking of the pleasure of salt water bathing and sunshine on one of these beaches, I am sure they will wish to return every year thereafter. Many of these beaches could be made more accessible and attractive by the owners themselves and at little cost.
I would commend the exploration of these resources especially to the municipalities as a field in which they could well increase their revenues at little or no cost. Local boards of trade also might well study the economic value of such developments to the locality concerned.
We in Nova Scotia are deeply grateful to this government for the special financial assistance which has enabled our municipalities more or less to hold the line in taxation and at the same time expand social, educational and health services. I am firmly convinced that under the positive policies of this government and the dynamic leadership of Premier Stanfield, Nova Scotia will continue to forge ahead even more rapidly than in the past year.

Will the hon. member do that? Of course he does not dare do it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are not in committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I recognize the hon. member for Beauce.
(Translation) :

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my contribution to the budget debate, may I take this opportunity to express my deepest sympathy to those of my constituents who have suffered hardship from the Chaudiere river floods. I know that a number of my constituents have again been affected this year and have sustained considerable lasses.
I cannot help sympathizing with them, and I also hope that those who are still worried will not suffer further losses, whether they are city dwellers or people with farms along the river banks.
I also hope that some agreement may be reached between the responsible government and the federal government to eliminate this annual danger.
Mr. Speaker, there is a very legitimate tradition for taxpayers, i.e. to wait with some anxiety and impatience for the budget speech because they want to know the policy of the government and the prospects for the coming year.
This year, as in the past, the Canadian taxpayer was wondering what changes would be introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), if any change was to be expected at all, as under this government, we have got used to annual deficits, which, of course, prevent the minister from providing any reductions in personal income tax.
The budget presented by the Minister of Finance on March 31, does not contain any important fiscal change, as the minister himself has admitted, but he is optimistic and hopes that 1960-1961 will show some improvement.
He believes, for instance, that Canadians will earn more and pay the government $1,750,000,000 in 1960, instead of $1,555,000,000 as in 1959.
This prosperity, according to the minister, will also extend to business corporations which will pay the federal treasury

$1,340,000,000 instead of $1,140,000,000 in 1959.
The minister also hopes that customs revenues will rise by $51 million during the next financial year and that the sales tax will also bring in $59 million more than in 1959.
Consequently, the greater portion of additional revenue which the government hopes to raise during the financial year 1960-61, i.e. an amount of $591 million, will come mainly from direct taxes on individuals and corporations, representing an amount of $395 million, i.e. a percentage of 66.
Individuals will therefore account for one third and corporation for another third of the additional income which the minister hopes to secure in order to reach a $12 million surplus.
I hope, as do all taxpayers, that those forecasts will materialize, because at that time, they would indicate improvement in our economy, at least from the point of view of gross national product.
But I am inclined to agree with my colleague for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson), that we will face another deficit and that the supplementary estimates will be higher than foreseen by the Minister of Finance.
Since this government has been in office, it is the first balanced budget that the Minister of Finance has attempted to introduce, and here again we will have to wait until next year to know whether he has achieved his ambition or if he has been over optimistic.
However, in spite of the minister's optimism, we can hardly forget that right now there are more than 800,000 unemployed in Canada.
We cannot forget either, that the net income of farmers decreased by 7 per cent in 1959.
Those are two fields for which the Minister of Finance does not foresee any rapid solution which could warrant his hopes for 1960-61.
In his budget speech, according to page 2685 of Hansard for March 31, 1960, under the heading Summary and Conclusions, the Minister of Finance admits that the total loss of revenue from the relieving amendments could add up to as much as $2 million, and he admits also that those changes represent only some corrections. Therefore, there are no exemptions, and the 1960-1961 budget is based merely on optimism, in so

far as the balancing of the budget is concerned. Supposing the hopes of the Minister of Finance do not materialize completely, 1 wonder what will happen to the unemployment insurance fund, because if business does not improve or at least does not improve sufficiently, there will still be unemployment unfortunately. We know that in the last fiscal year and during this one, the Conservative government has not taken, or does not want to take, any steps to eliminate the economic evil which is unemployment.
In agriculture, for the year 1960-61, will the government maintain support prices at their present level? We all know how much farmers are disappointed and anxious over the new system of deficiency payments. That is the reason why they have been urging the government to maintain support prices on butter and cheese, and to establish a new support price on milk powder. I sincerely hope that the government will give special consideration to these highly justified demands of farmers.
We also note that, in the last fiscal year, imports rose by 9 per cent, whereas exports increased only 5 per cent. This means that, from this angle, the Tory government has done nothing to reduce our trade deficit, and if the yield of customs duties in 1960-61 is $51 million more than last year's, as expected in the budget, it means that we can expect a further rise in our imports, and therefore our trade deficit will be still larger in the next fiscal year.
We, in Canada, have the facilities for greater production, because we have the manpower and the raw materials. What is lacking is markets. Yet, according to an item which appeared in Le Soleil for April 29, 1957, here is what the Prime Minister of Canada stated:
Mr. Diefenbaker accused the Liberal government of partly destroying our economic independence by allowing an unfavourable trade balance to accumulate between Canada and the United States, a balance which now reaches the figure of $11 billion, an all-time record, and by allowing foreign capital to invade Canada to such an extent that the Financial Post, that great business newspaper, wonders how long Canada can retain its separate entity, in view of the increasing control of foreign capital in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, those were the words of the Prime Minister in 1957. We are now in 1960, and he has been in power ever since that time, and yet he has not done a single thing as far as our trade deficit is concerned.
The Budget-Mr. Racine Here is what he said on the same subject in Brockville, on May 8, 1957, as reported by the Globe and Mail for May 19:
(Text):
In a major policy statement, John Diefenbaker tonight outlined the steps the Conservative party would take to counteract Canada's increasing unfavourable balance of trade and to assist small business.
Steps must be taken immediately, he said, to encourage the development of Canadian production to reduce and ultimately eliminate adverse trade balances.
To encourage trade, he underlined, Canadian individuals and institutions should be encouraged to participate to a greater extent in the equity ownership of foreign-owned Canadian corporations.
One of the best ways to produce this result, Mr. Diefenbaker added, would be the revision of taxation laws to encourage a larger degree of Canadian investment.
(Translation):
Those are the words of the leader of the Conservative party and, at the time, he surely did not know that the voters would try him out by electing him Prime Minister.
What is the Conservative government doing to alleviate this problem? Absolutely nothing.
In another field, we see that during the last fiscal year, the federal government paid over to the provinces $149,800,000 for hospital insurance purposes. This amount, for all practical purposes, comes from taxes collected by the federal government to be redistributed to the provinces under the hospial insurance plan.
It is unfortunate that the province of Quebec, while sharing in the costs of this program, does not yet share in its benefits.
This hospital insurance program came into operation, in fact, in 1959-1960, when all provinces except Quebec decided to participate.
In the province of Quebec, because of the inertia of the Union Nationale government, the measure has not yet gone beyond the study stage.
The financial situation of the government shows us also that expenditures increased by 6 per cent to a record amount of $5,706,800,000.
But here is what the Prime Minister had to say about this. According to the Toronto Telegram of May 2, 1957, which reported a speech made in Truro, Nova Scotia, the day before, he said:
(Text):
Mr. Diefenbaker pledged that a Conservative government would set up a commission similar to the Hoover commission in the United States so that the "unnecessary and wasteful federal expenditure could be eliminated."

The Budget-Mr. Racine (Translation):
And yet, since the Tory government has been in office, expenditures have kept going up.
Since the Conservatives got in, there has also been a money crisis; nobody can borrow except at prohibitive rates.
Yet in this regard, according to the London Free Press for June 7, 1957, the Prime Minister said in Woodstock on June 6:
(Text):
The Conservative leader criticized the government for its tight money policy which, he said, had paralysed the lumber industry, had levelled prosperity in certain provinces and had jeopardized or ruined small businesses.
(Translation):
And what about tight money? No later than April 7 last, we learned in La Presse that the school board of St. Johns, in the Iberville constituency, was refused a loan by a bank in St. Johns.
The article reads as follows:
The Iberville school board needed a $61,000 loan, but it was turned down by the bank with which it had been doing business, although permission to borrow had been granted by the municipal commission. This amount would have been used to pay interest dues on debentures and to pay the teachers' salaries.
It was to be a short term loan, to be repaid in December 1960. The board was counting on its taxes and statutory grants to repay it.
Mr. Speaker, you have there another vivid example of the difficulties encountered by our school boards and our municipal corporations when it comes to borrowing, even for the retirement of loans and urgent work projects.
I have referred to the case of that school board in particular but I must point out that this is by no means an isolated one. 1 only had to open a recent newspaper to see that similar cases are to be found everywhere.
The tight money situation affects all fields of our economy, including schools, municipalities and industry.
Think of the farmers who, as I said while speaking during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, went to the banks for loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act to buy tractors and were told that money was available to customers only. If that is not a tight money situation I wonder what is.
That is the kind of situation created for many of our farmers by the policy of a Tory government which has not tried to solve that problem.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the financial situation of our municipalities.

In the last few years, the federal and provincial governments have been increasing their taxes, while municipal taxes also went up pretty steadily every year in the form of higher land and sales taxes. Municipal corporations also have a budget to balance, and they only have one field of taxation on which to rely, that is property taxes, a fact which the other governments seem to worry very little about.
I feel that the provincial governments, as well as the federal government, should seek an answer to various municipal problems.
I do not wish to suggest that our governments should meddle with the internal affairs of our municipalities, but I think that the federal government could exempt our municipalities from the excise tax.
I know that many items are now tax-free, but this tax exemption should not cover those items only, but also all purchases that municipalities must make during the year.
Many reasons would justify such a policy on the part of the federal government. In the first place, the federal government does not pay any taxes and, second, the taxes it imposes are deductible for income tax purposes.
We may also consider that taxes collected by the federal government are subject to collection charges. Now, in the present case, collection charges have not been reduced because the government must still control items only, but also all purchases that munici-tax.
In my opinion, if it has been found advisable not to tax some specific items, this excise tax abatement should be extended to all purchases made by our municipalities.
As I was saying, I am entirely against the federal government intruding or interfering in the internal affairs of municipal administration.
However, since the Prime Minister will convene a federal-provincial conference very soon, we are justified in asking ourselves what part municipal representatives will play at this meeting.
The Prime Minister declared on March 28, in this house, that a federal-provincial conference would take place on July 25, 26 and 27. Following that announcement the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked the Prime Minister, in view of previous statements with regard to the matter, what would be the municipal participation in the conference. We are still waiting for the

Prime Minister's answer. Consequently, it is quite plausible to think that municipalities will have no say at that gathering.
If the government realizes the present position of municipal corporations, if it is aware of the trouble it caused them by grabbing all available funds to cover its own deficits, it has, in return and in all fairness, the responsibility of granting them full deduction of the excise tax on all their purchases.
Of course what I am advocating for municipal corporations I also want for school boards, for they are now in a position which is similar, if not worse.
In fact, practically every week we read in newspapers about the troubles of many school boards. At times, they even have to face strikes by teachers whose salaries they are unable to pay.
If I am urging the federal government to remove this excise tax, it is not only because I consider it could thus be of help without interfering in the municipal and school fields, but I consider it could in this way legitimately subsidize, under the constitution, the requirements of those municipal and school boards that are now in great need.
Mr. Speaker, you will perhaps find it strange that I should emphasize the fact that the deduction could be made without interference by senior governments, but precisely, I consider it an advantage to be able to help them without asking them anything in return, as a certain Quebec government is doing when it infiltrates itself into those corporations to better control them for political purposes.
It was rather amusing to note how certain Conservative members tried to make the best possible use of this debate on the budget.
The first one to do so was the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell) who, following the custom established by the Conservatives, did not fail to ask suggestions from the opposition. The Conservatives keep asking:	"What would
you do?" As if they were not the ones who had to fulfil the many promises they made to the Canadian voters.
The Conservative member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) stated, according to page 2905 of Hansard, that this was the most sensational budget that we could hope for as far as textile products are concerned, and he went on to say:
This last budget has caused enthusiasm in cities where the textile industry will now become prosperous.
That is not the kind of comment we read in La Presse for April 1, in which it is reported that the reaction of representatives of the
The Budget-Mr. Racine textile industry ranges from dissatisfaction to resignation, and that they are disappointed because the protective tariffs for this industry have not been raised high enough.
As for the Conservative member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais), he said very little about the budget. He chose instead to praise the Union Nationale, thereby forgetting that the subject matter of the debate was the budget of the Minister of Finance, his Conservative colleague.
He went on to give us the old story which is well known in the province of Quebec, and told us about the number of schools that were built not by the ratepayers, those who pay taxes, but by the Union Nationale, a party of Conservative trend, as he said according to page 2949 of Hansard.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay), as if it were appropriate for him to do so, took the opportunity to give us a lesson in ethics.
We conclude from this budget that the Conservatives hope that spring will bring about a solution to the unemployment problem; otherwise, as the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) stated, if spring does not bring any solution, the fund will be depleted by 1962.
We also note from the budget that there is nothing to show that the Conservatives intend to keep the promises they made to Canadian voters in the last two elections.
We note that there is nothing to show that farmers can expect a rise in their incomes, which dropped 7 per cent in 1959.
We note further that housebuilders are concerned, according to a statement made on April 4 by the chairman of their association in Montreal, and I quote:
The housebuilding industry, Mr. Holmes stated is now going through a very serious crisis, such as it has not known for a number of years.
In the first three months of 1960, he added, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation approved four times less mortgage loans than in the corresponding period last year. This year, it has approved 2,800 loans across Canada, as against 8,900 last year.
Mr. Holmes blames the situation on three factors: the attitude of C.M.H.C., the refusal of banks to grant mortgage loans; and the increasing indifference of lending firms.
The housebuilders association realizes that it is up against competition from industry and business, which are more attractive to moneylenders because they offer a higher rate of interest, whereas the rate is generally restricted to 6 per cent on mortgage loans for housing purposes.
Civil servants are also dissatisfied because their demands have only been partially met, and because the salary increases apply only to certain classes. Postal employees will not

The Budget-Mr. Ricard be satisfied, since this salary increase does not apply to them; in fact, those 20,000 postal employees, or so, are not included in the 50,000 civil servants who will benefit from an increase retroactive to April 1.
In other words, nobody, except Conservative members, seem to be satisfied with the administration of this government, and if, here and there, we hear rumours about the Conservatives going to the polls in 1961, perhaps it might be a good thing to suggest to them that they do it as soon as possible, because the people would be ready to get rid of them this very year.

Mr. Speaker, allow me, at the beginning of my remarks, to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on the efficient way in which he fulfils his task as Canada's great treasurer. The balanced budget he introduced in the house, on March 31 last, is evidence of his great ability and, at the same time, of the firm determination of the present Conservative government to give the country a sound economic leadership.
I was glad to hear, the other night, the Minister of Finance open his speech with the following words, uttered in my mother tongue:
In presenting my first budget on June 17, 1958, I drew attention to the fact that never since confederation, had any portion of the budget speech been delivered in this house in the French tongue, I expressed my surprise that in a parliament with two official languages enjoying complete equality every portion of this budget speech has always been delivered in English.
As a member of a constituency where 99 per cent of the people are French speaking, I think it is my duty to thank very sincerely the Minister of Finance for this courtesy towards the racial group to which I belong. His attitude confirms the determination of the present Conservative government to give the French language the place it rightfully deserves in the proceedings of our nation's parliament.
Mr. Speaker, when the minister spoke the words I quoted a moment ago, I stole a glance at my Liberal friends, sitting on my right, who never miss a chance to ask questions whenever anyone makes some slight error or a minor slip.
It was most amusing to see how humiliated and disappointed they were after the lesson the Minister of Finance had taught them. The lesson was the harder to swallow as it came from a member of a Conservative government


which in the past, they used to represent as the arch-foe of everything French Canadian. Therefore, in the days following the budget speech, our hon. friends, the Liberals, did not particularly try to play up this incident in the press. They chose instead to minimize the whole thing.
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the speeches made by hon. opposition members since the beginning of the session, and more particularly since the budget speech. I was surprised to see how upset they were by the minister's budget speech on March 31 last. It was particularly sad to witness the superhuman effort of my good friend and desk-neighbour, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), trying to criticize the budget submitted by the Minister of Finance. It was certainly a thankless task, as he had to criticize a budget which was most welcome to the remainder of Canadians.
Our people heard with great pleasure that there had been no tax increase. Textile workers in my district and in the remainder of the province rejoiced about tariff protection which, following the report of the tariff board, was announced in the budget speech. And now, Mr. Speaker, allow me to quote from an item, i.e. part of an article published by Le Courrier de Saint-Hyacinthe on the budget presented by the Minister of Finance. The title, and I quote, is:
A balanced budget In Ottawa. Forecast of a $12 million surplus.
The budget presented by the Hon. Donald Fleming, Minister of Finance in the cabinet of the Hon. John Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada, is full of optimism, dispels all gloomy forecasts, and hushes all the cries of dismay and hypocritical innuendoes of the Liberal opposition.
Not only does it forecast a surplus for the new financial year, but it reassures the people in respect of the question marks which are always present at this time of the year with regard to taxes and taxation.
Further on, it reads:
The strange thing is that the Liberal politicians who proclaimed themselves infallible throughout the country, failed, in their smug complacency to rouse themselves to an awareness of imminent economic perils.
Though they had been warned by their own financial and business experts, who were cautioning them against a future which might cause some uneasiness, they did not even take the trouble to listen to them nor to attempt any preventive gesture.
If we were to believe my hon. friends in the opposition, Canada is a rather poor country where life is rather dismal and hard. According to them, there is nothing

in Canada but unemployment and extreme misery caused by a tremendous load of taxes and duties.
That is the picture.
To listen to Liberal speeches-
That is right.

Industries are declining,
farmers are facing ruin, workers lead a miserable existence on the verge of bankrupty and so on.
According to them, these are the blackest years Canada and Canadians ever knew.
So they are, so they are.
On the other hand, if we were to believe the Liberals, there has never been either progress, or prosperity or happiness in Canada under any but their own rule.
That is right; it is true.
They alone are responsible for all beneficial legislation enjoyed by Canadians. All good comes from them.
And so it does.
And all evil, all that is wrong, is blamed on the Tories.
That's true, that's it.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal
troubadours, in their dirges-
The troubadours-

-make the most of a few weaknesses in our economy. They have not a word for the action taken by this government to correct the poor situation we inherited in June 1957. They are particularly careful not to go back any farther than the last world war. They boast about extraordinary and essential accomplishments under their regime and claim credit for a prosperity which was unavoidable in wartime.
They like to refer to the prosperity which prevailed under Liberal administration and made it possible for them to reach a high level of employment.
Our Liberal friends, while tooting their own horns, quite intentionally forget something. During the next few minutes, I should like to refer to those very details which they chose to leave out of their speeches.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal members did not utter a word about conditions that prevailed during the years 1926, 1927, 1928, 1929, 1936, 1937, 1938 and up to 1939 when the war got
The Budget-Mr. Ricard them out of the mess they were in. Farmers remember that in 1928 and 1929, hogs were selling at $4.50 a hundredweight, eggs at 8 to 10 cents a dozen, and butter at about 20 cents a pound.
When was that price for butter?

On the other hand, workers that are over forty today well remember that, at that time, there was a good deal of unemployment, that it was very hard for heads of families to find work and earn a living and that they had to be satisfied with wages of 10, 15 or 25 cents an hour.
The Liberal members might have added that verse to their dirge.
I have looked through Hansard-

-and I found that, at the
time, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) was not getting up every morning to ask the Minister of Labour if the number of unemployed had increased during the night. Oh, no, it was at the time of the Liberals, when there were 600,000 unemployed.
The situation is much more serious now. That is why.

Ten per cent of the labour force was unemployed, and our Liberal friends were sleeping, sleeping a deep sleep. At that time, therefore, they were ignoring the workers but now that they have lost the power, they just love the workers. Yes, they love them so much they are pressing them closely on their hearts so as not to hear their impressions on the conditions which prevailed when they were in power.
Here, Mr. Speaker, in support of what I just said, I would refer to a passage from a book entitled: "Official History of the Canadian Army, Six Years of Wars", by Stacey.
(Text):
I quote from page 112:
Another factor, probably less important in practice, made conscription seem unnecessary in Canada in 1939. The country had not fully recovered from the depression which had begun a decade before, and there was still a great deal of unemployment. Estimates of the number of unemployed at the outbreak of war run as high as 600,000, and the federal government at this time was still making large contributions to unemployment relief.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out again that that was under a Liberal government.
Mr. Speaker, in contrast with the dark picture presented by the Liberal members of the present economic situation, I

The Budget-Mr. Ricard should like to make a brief review of what has been done by the present Conservative government since it has been in office.
In the field of agriculture, which is the most important basic industry of this country, legislation was introduced right at the first session in order to correct a situation which was detrimental to the agricultural class. The farm price support act, which farmers had been expecting for a long time, was adopted in order to stabilize the prices of farm products. In order that the act, designed to help farmers, might be applied efficiently, a revolving fund of $250 million was set up.
Mr. Speaker, you will no doubt be glad to learn that, as a result of the policy adopted by the government which I have the honour to support, on price support, farmers of my constituency have received more than $262,000.
The sugar beet industry has enjoyed a support price from which it gained an amount of $41,390.70; the subsidy of 25 cents per hundredweight of processed milk, in ten dairying establishments, has yielded to the farmers an amount of $221,523.04. Added to that are deficiency payments on hogs and eggs, which will be paid later in the year.
An amount of $345 million was voted to pay cash advances to western farmers for farm stored grain. Those surpluses had piled up almost entirely under the Liberal administration.
The Canadian Farm Loan Act has been greatly improved. Under the former act, the maximum loan was $15,000, as against the present amount of $20,000, and the percentage of the loan has been raised from 65 to 75 per cent of the assessed value of the farm.
In July 1959, the Conservative government enacted the crop insurance act. The Animal Contagious Diseases Act was also amended to give greater compensation to farmers whose animals are slaughtered under a tuberculosis and brucellosis control program. Mention should finally be made of the amendment to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. An amount of $300 million was voted for that purpose.
One has to be extremely biased to claim that the present Conservative government has done nothing for the farmers. It has done more in three years than our predecessors in the 15 years before their defeat.
Now let us look at the working class. Let me mention first that an act was passed granting paid vacations to all workers under federal

jurisdiction. The unemployment insurance regulations were amended to remove any discrimination against married women. In 1957, an amount of $13 million was paid to 250,000 workers when the period of seasonal benefits paid under the unemployment insurance act was extended from 16 to 24 weeks. Then another extension was granted in 1958, which enabled approximately 200,000 workers to receive an additional amount of $14 million in benefits.
Again in the field of unemployment insurance, the benefit period was extended to 52 weeks, to help workers who are forced to remain idle because of the unavailability of jobs.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, may I make a few remarks on economic conditions prevailing in Canada, and particularly in my constituency, just to brighten up our friends in the Liberal party, who see everything through dark glasses. I should like to draw to the attention of the house certain indications of Canada's economic recovery, and just to prove my point, I shall quote from articles which appeared in various newspapers.
For instance, in La Presse of Tuesday March 22, 1960, we find the following:
Canadian companies will pay out this month in dividends an amount of $81,583,100, as compared to $77,878,900 in 1959 and $75,628,100 in 1958; the first quarter total reaches $195,794,000, that is 4 per cent more than in 1959 and 5 per cent more than in 1958, according to figures compiled by J. R. Timmins & Co.
Industrial firms are accounting for $48,444,000, a little more than last year but a little less than two years ago.
Due to the increase of the dividends of the International Nickel Company, the mines will distribute $21,979,200 this year, against $19,929,200 in 1959 and $17,119,100 in 1958.
Public utilities and financial institutions will pay out a little more this year than in the two previous years.
And, Mr. Speaker, here is an article from the Gazette of April 8 1960:
(Text):
Greater Activity is Shown in Manufacturing Industry.
A further improvement in manufacturing and processing activity, following a significant increase in February, is reported for March by the Canadian association of purchasing agents.
New orders were higher than in February, according to 37 per cent of the association's respondents.
(Translation):
And a little futher on it states:
(Text):
Employment edged ahead in the latest month with 23 per cent reporting more employees, more than offsetting the 17 per cent reporting a decrease.

(Translation):
In Le Devoir of April 6, 1960, I find the following:
Bright outlook for Ford of Canada.
Though sales so far in 1960 have not been as good as expected, it will be a good year however, said Mr. Rhys M. Sale, president of Ford of Canada, at the annual meeting of the shareholders.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with things which concern more particularly my district and, to do so, I will quote from Le Devoir of March 25, 1960:
Construction of a $15 million plant in Tracy.
Work will start this spring on the construction of a $15 million plant in Tracy, near Sorel, for the British Titan Products (Canada) Ltd.
The plant will have a capacity of 23,000 tons of titanic oxide a year and will require a regular working force of 250 people.
I read now from page 15 of Le Yamaska of March 9, 1960, the following title: "Southern Canada Power declares a 9.2 per cent increase for its gross revenue. The subhead reads:
More than one million kilowatt-hour sold. Sixty-four new industries established in this area in 1959.
You hear that, Mr. Speaker; 64 new industries. It is quite different from the gloomy picture that the members of the opposition are constantly describing.
In the speech he made last week, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) dealt with the textile industry and tried to make us believe that this industry started to decline in 1957 only, after the Conservative government assumed power.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record some information with regard to the textile industry. This is an excerpt from the publication Quebec Industriel of May 1957 On page 16, it says:
Employment in the primary textile industry has fallen from 98,000 in 1951 to 81,000 in 1956.
If my memory does not fail me, Mr. Speaker, I think that our hon. friends from the Liberal party were then in power. Therefore, the textile industry had begun to decline in their time. A little farther down, on the same page, we read:
Whereas in 1955 the total amount of profits for Canadian corporations were slightly higher than in 1950, those of the textile industry had fallen to about a third of what they were.
On page 18 we find:
And as the salary factor represents a significant proportion of production costs-costs being what they are in Canada-it is a stimulant to importation.
That was still under Liberal rule, Mr. Speaker.
That is why, from 1950 to 1954, approximately 70 companies had to close down, which resulted in the lay-off of 21,000 workers.
We did not hear the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) say
The Budget-Mr. Ricard anything about that. No, it could not be, because orders or rather the watchword of the party requests its members to present an entirely gloomy picture of things under Conservative rule.
Yet, I take much pleasure in referring again to the publication I already mentioned, and in quoting the title on page 24:
A disastrous tariff policy.
That was again under the Liberal government of the time, and it says:
For the last 20 years (except for the depression period of the 30's) there has been a gradual decline in Canadian tariffs on textiles from abroad: in fact, those of 1954 were lower than those of 1928. The decline was even higher than that of any other country. Consequently, our imports have increased at a faster rate than our production. The part of the national market that domestic production has satisfied has decreased from 67 to 57 per cent from 1950 until this year-
That is to say 1957, under a Liberal regime,
-while it was 71 per cent in 1930.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are a few bits of information that my friend, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska could probably have given the house.
I have never denied it. I even pointed it out myself. I said that the Gotham Hosiery, which lost its markets because it so stubbornly persisted in making full-fashioned hosiery that other firms took over the market, and when it was ready to switch to seamless hosiery- which women prefer-it was just too late, the market had been taken over by its competitors. He promised that taxes would be cut by $400 million. Income tax was to be reduced by $275 million, with a special deal for newly-weds; the

excise tax on cars was to be abolished with a tax saving of $60 million; corporation taxes on small businesses were to be reduced by $25 million and so on.
And this was to be done while increasing social security measures-sickness insurance, old age pensions for unmarried women at 60, family allowances to children up to 18 years of age. No suggestion was made for cutting expenditures through reduced services or by effecting economies.
There is no reason to believe that Mr. Pearson was not being completely sincere in his promises. If he had been elected to office it must be assumed that the tax cuts would have been made.
Thus it is fair to say that in 1958-59 there would have been a deficit of at least $400 million more than that reported by the Conservative government for the year. Instead of the Conservative deficit of $600 million, a government headed by Mr. Pearson would have had a deficit of more than $1 billion in 1958. Moreover, unless Mr. Pearson increased taxes drastically in 1959, he would have had a further deficit of more than $800 million for the 1959-60 fiscal year.
The Liberals would have made Mr. Fleming look like a piker in the deficit department. Naturally this would have involved much greater borrowing by a Liberal regime. Canada would have experienced tight money and inflation much more severe than anything seen during the past year.
This should be borne in mind when assessing the present bitter Liberal criticism of the Conservative financial record for the past two years.

Surely if it was true two years ago that the Liberal party was overtaxing by $120 a year, one way in which this government could have kept its promise to reduce taxes would have been to ascertain that the municipal taxes paid by the citizens of this country and paid toward the services they need-schools, sidewalks, waterworks- be deducted from federal income taxes. One group of citizens must pay to the three levels of government. It would have been easy for this government, in fulfilling the promises it made, to reduce taxes to permit citizens to deduct the municipal taxes they pay to that level of government from their income taxes.
