Mr. Speaker, I do not think I could add anything to the well deserved laurels that have been heaped on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). As we know, budgets are judged by time. I think history will record this as the finest budget for Canada that we have ever had.
I should like to take this opportunity of commending the young hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) for the marvellous contribution he made to this debate.
The other day the financial critic for the opposition, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), was referring to what the government had not done and among those things he included the fact that we had not set up a committee of research. He very kindly referred to me a couple of times because of my interest in research. I do not think it is necessary for me to remind him or the house that there is on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) a resolution to set up such a committee. I hope and expect that we shall have that committee functioning after the Easter recess.
I should also like to remind the hon. member who referred to this research problem that while we were in opposition for

The Budget-Mr. Murphy six years I tried to have a committee such as this set up; and on more than one occasion we could not even get a debate on the matter through the manoeuvring of the members of the then government.
I am one of those who are very proud indeed that we are going to have a committee set up-and I am sure it will be nonpolitical-to study not only the policies but also the administration of these three different bodies; Chalk River atomic energy commission, the national research council, and Eldorado Mining Company. I think a great deal of good could emerge from the discussions. I remember sitting on one of these committees studying different subjects years ago, and in the end that committee made one of the greatest contributions which, I imagine, any committee has ever made toward improved administration. I expect this group will do the same.
There are three items with which I should like to deal, two of them only briefly. We have heard recently about these airquakes, or the effect produced by planes which crack the sound barrier. We had an illustration here in Ottawa and there was another at Montreal a while ago. I am going to tell the house this: last fall one of these planes, apparently from Selfridge air base near Detroit, performed the same feat in my area. I happen to live on lake Huron, and a friend of mine telephoned to inquire about 30 feet of his bank which had dropped three or four feet. We had some geologists out there, and we ascertained the exact time of this drop. It was caused, according to these geologists, by this plane cracking the sound barrier. That drop of three to four feet, 30 feet back from the brow of the bank, extended for over two miles. I am going to suggest to this government that it is about time we took heed of this practice. It may be necessary but, if it is, let that practice be carried on where it is not going to do any damage. There are plenty of areas in the United States, as well as in Canada, where that can be done without flying over populated areas such as has been done on the three occasions I have mentioned.
The other item to which I wish to refer briefly has implications which discourage me very much. In the first speech I ever made in this house some 16 years ago I dealt with the tourist industry. As we all know, the set-up in this connection was introduced under Bennett and there has been a kind of autopsy ever since. We were informed recently that the revenue derived by Mexico from the United States in respect of the tourist industry exceeded the revenue received by Canada from the United States. To me that is very disturbing.


We are taking a very negative approach to this problem. We talk about trade deficits, and we have them. There is one way in which we could get another $500 million, and that is by developing the tourist industry. I think we have to make a more positive approach to this problem. Where I live I am within one day's drive, on the United States side of the border, of more people than are living in the whole Dominion of Canada, yet we are getting very little tourist traffic as I see it. Unless some change is made, we shall get even less.
On the same subject, a couple of years ago when they opened the new Canada House in New York, where the travel bureau had its office on the main floor, the United Kingdom travel bureau also had an office with about twice the space. Although Britain's revenue from United States tourists is less than ours, the United Kingdom is opening up more offices in the United States. As a matter of fact, the director for the United Kingdom received a citation-an order-from his government because of his success in promoting the tourist industry in the United States. I think the sooner we take an aggressive attitude toward the development of that industry the better it will be for our economy.
The other part of my speech deals with a subject which I think will concern many hon. members of this house. I referred a few moments ago to my living on lake Huron, one of the great lakes, which have an area of some 90,000 square miles. We were disturbed in that area on account of a platform which was being constructed by an oil and gas drilling company for the purpose of supporting drilling equipment to be used to drill for either oil or gas. The platform happened to be about 2,000 feet from the Sarnia shoreline and just a little farther from where the town has its water intake. As hon. members know, large areas of western Ontario obtain their water from lake Huron. I will say without hesitation that it is only a matter of 10 or 15 years before Georgian bay and lake Huron will be supplying water to the area from Toronto to Windsor, because it will be the only body of pure water left.
As I say, we were disturbed about this drilling operation because we knew what effect it would have upon the tourist industry, upon the beaches, upon fishing and upon health. As a matter of fact, I happened to get the idea that the company did not have the proper permit which is required in order to build a platform of that sort. The federal government can grant two types of permits and, as we also know, under the British North America Act the provinces control the land under the water but the federal government controls the water. On coming to

Ottawa to see the then new Minister of Public Works I was advised that the company did not, in fact, have the proper permit, and that the permit which had been granted was not transferable. Through the co-operation of the minister and through his action that platform was dismantled within a very few days and there have been no drilling operations attempted since.
My point is this: we are not satisfied. We know that on lake Erie there are some 13 gas and oil companies with licences and leases for drilling. We do not want that to happen on lake Huron or lake St. Clair. We feel- and rightly so-that these waters should be kept as pure as possible. The purity of these waters is more important than a few million extra barrels of oil or a few million extra cubic feet of gas, because we are certainly not short of gas and oil in this country, and we shall not be for centuries.
The government of Ontario, since Mr. Macauley took office as minister of natural resources, has taken a very active and constructive attitude with regard to this serious problem. Mr. Macauley set up a committee headed by Dr. Langford, one of the best known geologists on this continent, to make inquiries regarding oil and gas drilling on the great lakes. As a matter of fact, the committee is sitting in Sarnia during Easter week and it is also going to Lansing, Michigan. As hon. members may know, the Ontario legislature recently introduced some amendments to the energy act giving the government power to prohibit drilling for oil and gas in certain areas. What I am suggesting here is that this is the concern of several of our departments of government. Looking over the treasury benches I am reminded that almost every government department is affected including the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Transport, as well as, probably some others.
My suggestion is that the two governments now get together in view of the proposed legislation in Ontario and work out a solution so that there will not be any drilling in the areas in the great lakes where there is not now drilling and so that the existing leases will not be renewed when they expire in relation to those areas where they are now operating. In this way we will probably have a greater body of fresh water. It is amazing to learn upon reading some statistics that 15 of the great rivers in the United States are so polluted as to be unfit for use by humans. No chlorination is adaptable for the impurities of those streams.

I hope the government will take notice of this problem. The Navigable Waters Protection Act was first introduced, I believe, in 1882 or 1886. Certainly oil and gas drilling did not constitute a problem then because it had never occurred on the great lakes up to that time. I believe that legislation is due for an overhauling.
One fortunate aspect of the situation is that we are receiving excellent international co-operation. This matter began to brew in August and, as a matter of fact, a meeting was called at my suggestion by the mayor of Port Huron. He was being visited by some United States senators and others together with our mayor, the city manager and so on. Protests were sent by the governor of the state to Premier Frost and also to his own state department at Washington who alerted the Canadian Department of External Affairs with the result that they were represented at any hearings held before the Ontario fuel board.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on February 12 of last year announced that a national conference on conservation would be convened and several cabinet ministers have referred to the necessity for conservation not only in relation to water but in relation to land use and all that sort of thing.
There are also some very alert bodies on both sides of the border interested in this problem. We have the great lakes commission composed of members representing the states of Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Illinois. That body has been formed to conserve and develop the water resources of the area. They believe the time has come to require all ships, large and small, to have spillage collection and storage systems. Speaking of spillage from ships, I think this must be corrected. I believe that ships will have to be required to provide containers so that they may empty their spillage at the proper places and at the proper times.
We had an illustration of the need for this some few years ago in the Parry Sound district when one of the Imperial Oil Company tanks burst. As I recall it, it took three years to clean up the mess and finally a good deal of the sand had to be removed and replaced with fresh sand. If I remember correctly the cost to Imperial Oil Company was about $1,500,000.
While a person could speak indefinitely about pollution it is not my intention to do so. We had last summer a spillage of oil in lake Erie and the beaches were rendered practically useless. Not many miles from where the platform was built last fall in lake Huron there was a well on land in the state of Michigan that gushed. Over 100,000

If that had happened where the platform was being built the oil would have gone into the shipping channel of the river and with the amount of freight that passes up and down in that area it would have resulted in considerable damage to property and a considerable loss of life.
Here again, just a few weeks ago, we had another gusher. We had to send to Texas for one of the men whose business it is to cap wells. It is my contention that these experts could more easily cap a well on land than on water. While it has been the stated policy of the Ontario government that it will not permit any drilling in this area if there is any danger of pollution, I feel I should point out that no system of drilling has been perfect to date to such an extent that a drilling operation is free from pollution. It is useless for the government to say, "We will permit it as soon as we are satisfied there will not be any pollution." Our contention is that we simply should not take that chance.
Another aspect of this problem is the situation already confronting some of the cities. It is amazing to learn that some of the large United States cities have had to close their beaches because of pollution. What concerns me are the changes required in the Navigable Waters Protection Act because of the possibility of fire. Because we are now having such marvellous co-operation on the part of the government of the province of Ontario and the government of the state of Michigan and of the other states bordering on the great lakes, it is time for us to get together on a high level at a conference involving the two federal governments as well as the governments of the states and provinces concerned to bring our legislation up to date. Certainly it has needed revision for a long time.
I believe that you, Mr. Speaker, and indeed many hon. members in this house live not too far from lake areas. We have on the great lakes' system hydroelectric developments at Niagara Falls and along the St. Lawrence river which are among the world's largest. The shores and waters of the great lakes provide a vast fishing, hunting and recreation area for millions of people, both residents and tourists. I mentioned a while ago that the contamination of our beaches would crucify the tourist industry, and I am satisfied that it would. Expert evidence reveals that oil on the beaches becomes jellied and most difficult to dispose of. I referred to the instance at Parry Sound a few moments ago.
We have been supported, also, by some 75 municipalities in our efforts to prohibit drilling. The Canadian-United States water


pollution committee of which I have the honour to be chairman has appointed legal counsel to represent it at the hearings of the Ontario board on April 21. Counsel was directed by the executive to ask for the prohibition of drilling in lake Huron, lake St. Clair and the connecting waters. If we accomplish this we hope we can take action with respect to other areas such as lake Erie at a later date.
I am very glad to have the opportunity to bring this problem before the house. It is a serious one; it affects everybody. The water problem in this country and in this world is one of the greatest problems that we have to face. There is no question about that. The time to take action is now, before it is too late. Beaches that were good 10 or 15 years ago are not useable now, even in the large areas. I am sure that the many departments concerned, realizing the importance of avoiding any damage to property or loss of life, will consider the episode which happened in Michigan within the last few months because, as I said before, and I repeat, if that had happened where the drilling platform was being erected it could have scuttled probably 100 ships in the St. Clair river since you can always stand on the bridge and see maybe 30 or 40 ships going one way or the other.
It is too serious a matter for us to ignore. With the co-operation of the different states and their willingness and determination to try and cure this evil, I think we can work together to obtain the necessary results.

Therefore, the government made me live over a year of deception, because it dealt with anything but what was important, necessary and urgent. This budget advises me moreover to be prepared for another similar year, a year of deception, since the budget is about the same.
There has been no change worth mentioning and we will go on living just as last year.
They will continue to play the administrator. Important problems will be put aside and will be left unsolved next year just as last year. They are playing and they will continue to play the administrator, but they will take great care of their publicity.
The important problems, to our Conservative friends, are to stay in power, take care of their publicity, control radio and television, visit the world, travel-this looks good in the newspapers and it seems truly important. But what good does it do to have consulates, agencies, paid representatives in different countries to take care of our affairs? The minister has to go there just the same, even if it is only to see if our representative is a Conservative or a Liberal.
And we will spend weeks dealing with the Jacques Cartier bridge issue. That is something to give work to our unemployed; that is something that will lower the national debt, the interest rate, the cost of living, the credit restrictions. That is not important. What they need is a little scandal so they can throw up a smoke screen to hide a bad administration. We will talk for days about capital punishment. Who discussed capital punishment during the last election campaign? Nobody. That matter had no importance then.
In 1956, a committee of members of parliament and senators of all parties reported on the matter after considering it for many months. The committee heard the evidence of jurists, of an executioner, of wardens, constables, policemen, etc., and came to the conclusion, in 1956, that capital punishment should remain on the statute books. Well, it happens now that this government, while there is unemployment, while the national debt and the cost of living are increasing,

The Budget-Mr. Denis extends the debate for one, two, three and four days more to deal with capital punishment. That is what is important to them, because it works as a smoke screen, helping to make us forget the bad administration of their government. Newspapers are full of articles about that; we are shown photos of the electric chair, photos of the scaffold, and everyone explains to us the reactions of the condemned, five minutes before he goes to the scaffold, five minutes before and after. That is what we are concerned with, instead of concerning ourselves-

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this sixth day of the budget debate there is little left to be said. I want to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) upon a job well done. To have taken over the financial difficulties which were building up prior to 1957 and to have balanced the budget in three years is an achievement of which the minister and this government can be very proud.
As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) stated in his address in the house, while the Minister of Finance had hoped to balance the budget this year, this has been accomplished. Commenting on this accomplishment, the hon. member for Greenwood stated as reported at page 3006 of Hansard:
I think as one looks back one can see that it has not come about by accident but was based on long term planning and tenacity.
I certainly agree with this statement. Judging from newspaper headlines and editorial comments the balanced budget has been well received in all parts of Canada. Most people realize that after the period of deficit financing that stopped the threat of recession, a balanced budget will bolster the confidence in the Canadian economy. Even opposition speakers have more or less admitted this fact through their more than moderate criticism in this budget debate.
Canada's financial growth is graphically illustrated in a chart which appeared in many newspapers across Canada and which was headed "Awakening Giant of the Twentieth Century". It shows a graph of the gross national product as it continues upward, and it has been climbing more steeply in the last two years. Underneath the chart are these words:
Nothing so dramatically reveals Canada in the role of the awakening giant of the twentieth century as a glance at the chart above which shows the spectacular jump by which the country's gross national product has soared upward.. .to a prodigious 34.5 billion in 1959.. .Canada has emerged from an industrial fledgling, bursting with purpose and activity, to take her place as one of the great industrial nations of the world.
The Budget-Mr. Pascoe
I suggest that it is the policies of this government and, as has been stated, the long term planning and tenacity of the Minister of Finance that have made this chart possible.
Comments from my own city of Moose Jaw in Saskatchewan indicate, I believe, the general opinion on the effect of the budget in this new fiscal year. I have here newspaper statements from interested parties. The president of the Moose Jaw chamber of commerce said that the budget semed to be a reasonable one. The secretary of the local branch of the joint action committee and secretary of the local of the civil service association of Canada said that he was most pleased with what he had heard about civil servants' pay. He added that it was a step in the right direction. I might add that prior to coming down here to Ottawa I had dealings with the civil service. I found them to be very reasonable. I told them that the Minister of Finance had said that when the occasion arose the government would treat the civil servants in the various categories as well as it was possible to treat them.
The first vice president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool who lives in Moose Jaw said, "There seems to be little in it for the farmers". From personal acquaintance with him I know he is a reasonable man; and I am sure he will admit that farmers as well as other segments of our economy will benefit from the confidence in our future inspired by a balanced budget.
The mayor of Moose Jaw said that he was glad that the taxes on the people had not been raised. He also said he hoped the statement that the government would be getting out of the money market as much as possible would help municipalities with their financial problems.
In connection with municipal financing, I should like to re-emphasize what others who have spoken have said about the greatly increased grants of money the federal government is now making to the provincial governments. The Minister of Finance outlined how much more money is now going to the provincial governments in the table which appears at page 2676 of Hansard. I should like to refer to that table for a moment. I will just outline the totals. This table shows unconditional payments, conditional payments and extra payments. The unconditional payments estimated for the new fiscal year 196061 total $870.1 million as compared with $552.7 million in 1956-57. The conditional payments estimated for this new fiscal year total $389 million as compared with $111 million in 1956-57, the last fiscal year of the Liberals. Then there are extra payments, such as

Business of the House university grants and grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal government property totalling $41.8 million as estimated for this new fiscal year as compared with $25.7 million in the 1956-57 fiscal year.
The grand total shows the picture much more plainly. In this fiscal year 1960-61 the federal government is giving to the provincial governments by way of grants $1,300.9 million compared with $689.4 million in 1956-57, the last year of the Liberal administration. In other words, the federal government is paying in grants this year almost double what was paid' by the Liberal government in the fiscal year 1956-57.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
When the house re-assembles on April 25 the order of business for that week will run as follows. Monday is a private members' day. On Tuesday we will start off with No. 8 on today's order paper, second
reading of Bill No. C-56, to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, followed by No. 9 on today's order paper which is second reading of Bill No. C-57, an act to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act. The third item is No. 10 on today's order paper, the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the tenure of office of judges. The fourth item would be the motion in the name of the Prime Minister to set up a select committee on the procedure of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What number is that item?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is item No. 15 on today's order paper. The fifth item is No. 11 on today's order paper, being the motion in my name to set up a select committee to consider the national research council and other matters as there outlined. Then those items of business being completed, we would continue with budget resolutions. That would be the business of the house for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
